claims.text: Chemical dealloying can produce noble-metal-based high-entropy-alloy three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
The process selectively etches less noble elements from a homogeneous alloy precursor.
Selective etching yields a porous, noble-metal-rich framework.
The porous noble-metal-rich framework exhibits enhanced catalytic performance.
The precursor has a homogeneous atomic distribution of noble and less noble metals.
Acidic or alkaline chemical treatment can selectively remove less noble metals from the precursor.
Appropriate pH, temperature, and reaction time favor dissolution of less noble elements while preserving the noble-metal framework.
Removal of less noble elements forms a self-supported, porous three-dimensional nanoframework.
The resulting framework has high surface area and fine noble-metal connectivity.
Selective dealloying operates through differences in electrochemical stability between noble and less noble metals.
Under controlled conditions, less noble metals dissolve preferentially.
Preferential dissolution leads to nucleation and growth of a porous, interconnected noble-metal network.
Selective dealloying improves atomic-scale uniformity within the resulting network.
The dealloyed nanoframework will have significantly higher catalytic activity than the original uniform alloy.
The dealloyed nanoframework will have greater catalytic stability than the original uniform alloy.
Increased surface area and optimized atomic arrangements of noble-metal sites cause the proposed improvements in catalytic activity and stability.
Successful framework formation requires a precursor composition that permits selective etching.
Excessively strong binding of less noble elements can prevent successful selective etching.
Overly aggressive dealloying conditions can collapse the framework or cause loss of compositional uniformity.
Atomic-level control and catalytic improvement depend on fine-tuning the dealloying parameters.
